An assistant skill is a packaged capability that extends what a broader assistant can understand and do. It usually defines a domain, supported intents, required entities, dialog behavior, and access to a relevant service.

A broad [[Personal Virtual Assistant]] must select the right skill through [[Intent Triggering]]. Once activated, the skill can use a narrower [[Intent Schema]] and task-specific [[Dialog Policy]].

An association rule is an implication from one itemset to another, written as an antecedent leading to a consequent. It summarizes how often the sets occur together in transaction data.

Support measures prevalence and confidence measures conditional co-occurrence. The rule is an observed association and does not by itself show causation.

An asymmetric game gives players different starting conditions, rules, roles, resources, or victory conditions. Fairness depends on the total opportunities each side receives rather than identical components.

Asymmetry can create distinctive strategies and cooperation, but it is harder to tune. A unique ability becomes unfair when its advantages are not offset by meaningful costs, limitations, or opposing tools.

An asynchronous assistant can continue a task after the immediate conversational turn and return when a result or event becomes available. The user does not have to hold an open synchronous exchange while external work completes.

The [[Dialog Manager]] must preserve task state, associate a late result with the correct request, and choose an appropriate time and channel for notification. This behavior often overlaps with [[Proactive Assistant|proactive interaction]].

An asynchronous controller action returns a task and awaits asynchronous repository or service operations. While an external operation is incomplete, the request does not need to occupy a thread that can perform no useful work.

This can improve server scalability under concurrent I/O-bound requests, but it does not make the underlying database operation intrinsically faster. The asynchronous path should extend through the dependencies rather than blocking inside them.

An asynchronous validator evaluates a form rule whose result is not available immediately. It returns a future result, commonly through an [[Observable]], and leaves the control pending until that result arrives.

A duplicate-name validator can call a server endpoint because uniqueness depends on stored records rather than the current browser model. The request should be controlled to avoid sending a new server check for every unnecessary keystroke.

An atomic challenge is the immediate, indivisible obstacle facing a player during play. It is the lowest level in a [[Hierarchy of Challenges]] and is not composed of smaller subchallenges.

Atomic challenges combine into larger tasks such as encounters, sub-missions, and levels. Their sequence and overlap determine the moment-to-moment texture and difficulty of gameplay.

An atomic operation appears indivisible to competing threads: no observer sees it half-complete. .NET's `Interlocked` operations provide atomic increments, exchanges, additions, and compare-and-swap behavior for selected primitive locations.

Atomic primitives avoid a full lock for small state transitions, but they do not automatically protect a larger invariant spanning several values. Correct lock-free design requires the entire algorithm, not just one assignment, to remain valid under every interleaving.

An attention mechanism lets a neural model assign different importance to different parts of its input while producing an output. Instead of forcing all information through one fixed summary, it builds a context weighted toward what is currently relevant.

In an [[Encoder-Decoder Network]], attention helps align an output word or symbol with the input positions that support it. The weights are learned with the rest of the network.

Kelleher presents attention-centered transformer models as an alternative to relying on one fixed sentence vector: the model can dynamically focus on selected input parts while generating an output. He also describes BERT's use of an unlabeled-data pretraining stage followed by smaller task-specific supervised tuning. These were developments discussed in the book's 2019 outlook, not a claim about which architecture currently leads every task.

An attribute selector matches elements by the presence or value of an attribute. Operators can require an exact value or test whether a value begins with, ends with, contains, or includes a whitespace- or hyphen-separated token.

This lets CSS respond to information already present in the document without adding a class. A case-insensitivity flag can alter value comparison where supported, while the document language still determines how attribute names and values behave.

An attribute's measurement type constrains sensible arithmetic and comparison. Nominal values distinguish categories without order; ordinal values have an order but not necessarily equal distances; numeric interval values admit meaningful differences, while ratio values also have a meaningful zero and ratios.

Encoding categories as numbers does not make their numeric distances real. A model or transformation that averages arbitrary category codes can introduce relationships absent from the domain. Choosing a data representation therefore includes checking what operations the values actually justify.

An attributed graph associates properties with its vertices, edges, or both. The topology expresses relationships while attributes carry types, labels, weights, identifiers, or application data used by queries and updates.

Accelerators must fetch and interpret these values as well as traverse adjacency, so property layout and memory access can be as important as the edge representation.

An attribution map displays which inputs or internal activations a neural network relies on for a particular output. Kelleher describes saliency or heat-map views that estimate how strongly the output relates to neurons in earlier layers.

This helps inspect a decision pathway in a large network whose representations are distributed across many units. The map is a model-analysis aid, not an exact human-readable chain of reasoning or proof that the model used only the highlighted information. Alongside [[Neural Feature Visualization]], it addresses part of the [[Neural Network Explainability Gap]] by making internal contributions easier to examine.

An audio bank is a packaged collection of authored sound events, samples, and metadata loaded by an audio middleware system. Banks let the game request logical events without constructing every DSP setting or asset path in code.

The audio system loads required banks during startup or content transitions and unloads them when no longer needed. Event names and bank versions become a contract between the audio-authoring project and the engine.

An audio bus groups sound events into a mix category such as music, dialogue, effects, or ambience. Changing a bus affects every routed event, allowing independent volume control, muting, or processing without visiting each instance.

Buses can form a hierarchy so a master bus governs the full mix while child buses retain category control. An [[Audio Snapshot]] can change several bus settings together for a temporary game state.

An audio snapshot is an authored set of temporary mix and effect changes applied across one or more [[Audio Bus|buses]]. Activating it can lower music, emphasize dialogue, add reverb, or otherwise reshape the mix for a situation.

Snapshots can fade in and out rather than switching abruptly. Because they modify routing state rather than replacing every sound, existing event instances continue playing through the transition.

An auditory display is an [[Output Device]] that presents information through hearing. In a [[3D User Interface]], a major goal is [[Spatial Audio]] that allows a listener to localize the direction and position of a sound.

Audio can indicate off-screen objects, support [[Wayfinding]], provide ambient realism, substitute for missing touch feedback, encode data through [[Sonification]], or deliver annotation and help. It can be presented through headphones or external speakers, each with different tradeoffs involving comfort, isolation, crosstalk, externalization, and support for multiple listeners.

In AR, generated sound can be spatially registered with a physical source or location and mixed with the sounds already present in the environment. This makes auditory augmentation useful when an object lies outside the visual field or when additional graphics would overload the display.

An augmented matrix places the [[Coefficient Matrix]] and right-hand-side vector of a [[Linear System]] side by side, written $[A\mid b]$.

[[Elementary Row Operation|Elementary row operations]] on this matrix represent equivalent operations on the equations. Its echelon form reveals consistency, free variables, and the solution.

An authenticated user is the identity established after the server validates the credentials or token attached to a request. ASP.NET Core makes that principal and its claims available to controller code.

For a write operation, the server can derive authorship from this validated identity rather than trusting a user identifier supplied in the request body. That binds persisted ownership to authentication evidence.

An authored story is a deliberately shaped narrative carried by a game. Its creator arranges plot, characters, context, rules, images, words, animation, and sound to communicate particular events or ideas.

Authorship can range from a fixed story shown alongside play to a story expressed through the playable system itself. It does not exclude player action, but the available material and paths are intentionally provided by the creator.

An authorization policy is a named set of requirements that an authenticated request must satisfy before protected ASP.NET Core code runs. A controller or action can reference the policy declaratively instead of repeating access checks in its body.

Policies keep permission logic separate from HTTP coordination and can be reused across endpoints. Authentication establishes the principal evaluated by the policy; it does not by itself guarantee authorization.

An autocorrelation feature measures the association between a time series and lagged versions of itself. Values at selected lags reveal repetition, persistence, and characteristic temporal scales.

A collection of lag correlations can distinguish dynamics even when two series have similar marginal distributions. Interpretation must account for trend and nonstationarity, which can create high correlations without a stable repeating mechanism.

An autoencoder is a neural network trained to reconstruct its input at its output. An encoding hidden layer transforms the input into an internal representation, and a decoding layer uses that representation to rebuild the original values.

The architecture must avoid a trivial copy path if its representation is to be informative. Kelleher gives a narrower hidden layer as one bottleneck: the network has to retain useful structure while discarding some redundant information. [[Layer-Wise Autoencoder Pretraining]] once used successive encoders to initialize deep networks, though the book notes that most deep networks no longer require that particular procedure.

As a feature learner, the encoder maps observations into a latent representation while the decoder supplies a reconstruction objective. Sparse, denoising, stacked, and variational variants constrain that representation in different ways.

An autologous cell source uses cells taken from the same person who will receive the engineered tissue. Immune recognition is generally more favorable than with cells from an unrelated donor.

The source may still be limited by patient health, harvest size, expansion time, cost, and whether the required cell type can be obtained or differentiated reliably.

An automated Blender still-render pipeline prepares materials, lights, a scene camera, image dimensions, and an output path before invoking a render operation that writes the image. The camera must be assigned to the scene, since the full renderer uses that camera to determine the frame.

The source contrasts a full Blender render with an OpenGL snapshot of the 3D Viewport. The full render includes the scene's lighting and material result at higher computational cost; the viewport render captures a faster working view and can use the user's current viewing context. Both become reliable only after the script controls their required scene state.

An automated playthrough drives a game through scripting or replay data so integrated behavior can be checked without continuous human input. Assertions can detect crashes, failed progress, performance violations, or outcomes outside an expected range.

It covers longer paths than a unit test while remaining repeatable. Human testing is still required for unanticipated behavior and experiential quality.

An automated test executes a repeatable scenario and checks an observed result against an expected result without manual inspection. It can target a function, a server boundary, or a complete browser workflow.

Automation shortens feedback only when the result is dependable. Test scope, controlled setup, meaningful assertions, and cleanup determine whether a failure points toward the behavior that changed.

An autonomic security system can monitor its own condition, identify harmful behavior, choose a response, and restore operation with limited human intervention. The model aims for self-protection and self-healing when attack speed exceeds manual response.

Autonomy requires bounded actions, trusted observations, and recovery safeguards so that a false alarm does not cause greater damage than the threat. [[Computer Immunology]] provides one conceptual basis for this adaptive behavior.

An autonomous photovoltaic plant serves a local network without relying on a central grid as its main supply. The source's layout combines a [[Solar Array]], storage battery, charge controller, inverter, and standby diesel generator. Solar generation, battery discharge, and backup generation must together cover load and internal losses. Remote homes, pumps, and telecommunications sites are example applications.

An autonomous physical system uses processed information to act in the material world without requiring a person to approve every operation. Connected vehicles, industrial devices, and other automated equipment join data analysis to physical consequences.

Governance must therefore examine sensing, processing, control, and accountability as one chain. An error in [[Automated Information Collection]] or interpretation can become movement, restriction, or damage rather than remaining a mistaken record.

An autonomous power plant uses local energy sources to provide electricity at or near its point of demand. The source lists solar, wind, biomass, and small run-of-river hydro as possible inputs, often assembled into a hybrid with standby generation. Local supply avoids long-distance transmission loss, while intermittent sources require backup, storage, or both. See [[Autonomous Photovoltaic Plant]] for one specific arrangement.

An autotelic experience is pursued because the activity and its goals are rewarding in themselves. The motivation is intrinsic to taking part rather than supplied only by an external necessity or prize.

[[Flow]] often makes an activity autotelic by aligning challenge, skill, goals, and feedback. Games also support autotelic play when players create personal [[Player Goal|goals]] that remain meaningful within the available systems.

An auxiliary sweep repeats a study step across values of one or more auxiliary parameters. It is useful when parameter continuation should occur within the solver sequence or when combinations of inputs must be explored alongside the primary study definition.

Continuation can also help a nonlinear problem converge by solving an easier condition first and using that solution as the initial estimate for the next value. The resulting family should still be checked for failed cases and interpreted like a [[Parametric Sweep in COMSOL|controlled parameter study]].

An avatar is the fictional character, vehicle, or other entity through which a player is represented in the game world. The player may identify with it as an imaginary self even when it is not human.

Avatar design affects both mechanics and interpretation. Its available actions define what the player can do, while appearance, voice, history, and behavior shape the kind of identification the game invites.

An avatar-based interaction model lets the player influence the world through one represented character, vehicle, or entity. The player's reach is limited to the avatar's location and permitted actions.

The interface must support movement, orientation, object use, and awareness from that situated position. Camera and navigation choices are tightly coupled because the player often cannot see the whole world at once.

An average-comparison time plot places a series beside a relevant mean and may also show their difference. A long-term seasonal average can expose unusually high or low periods that the raw [[Time Plot]] alone makes hard to judge. The reference and deviation should be visually distinguishable, and a separate screen for the difference can prevent the baseline from obscuring the original values. A [[Horizon Graph]] can compactly display those deviations.

An axially loaded member is a rod-like structural component whose applied forces act along its longitudinal axis. Under the small-deformation assumptions used in the primer, the member primarily develops normal stress and axial displacement.

A one-dimensional bar mesh models this behavior with translational nodal degrees of freedom. Constant, varying, and stepped cross sections change how stiffness and stress are distributed along the member.

An axis-aligned bounding box, or AABB, is a rectangular collision volume whose sides remain parallel to the world coordinate axes. It can be represented by minimum and maximum values on each axis.

Two AABBs intersect when their intervals overlap on every relevant axis. The test is efficient, but a rotating object may require the box to grow or be recomputed because the box itself does not rotate with the object.

An Azure App Service plan defines the compute capacity and hosting tier used by one or more App Services. The web applications run within the resources allocated by that plan rather than owning independent servers directly.

The plan is therefore a capacity and cost decision for the hosted application. Client and backend services may share a plan when that arrangement fits their environment and demand.

An Azure application setting is a named configuration value supplied by App Service to the hosted process. It lets deployment provide environment-specific URLs, feature values, and other configuration without rebuilding source code.

The setting name must match what the application configuration reads. Slot-specific settings can remain attached to staging or production when application versions are swapped between them.

An Azure deployment slot is a separately addressable App Service environment associated with an application. A release can be deployed to a staging slot and exercised there before the slot is swapped into the production position.

Slots reduce the need to replace production files in place. Settings must be classified carefully so environment-specific values remain with the intended slot during a swap.

An Azure Function is a small stateless unit of code invoked by a configured trigger and hosted with managed scaling. The developer supplies the operation while Azure supplies and scales the execution infrastructure, which is why the model is described as serverless.

The book's C# function compares dates for a logic app and returns a compact result. A function is useful when a high-level workflow reaches a calculation that is clearer or more reliable in ordinary code.
